name: Daria Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do certified translations from Arabic into English, mostly birth certificates, marriage papers, diplomas and bank statements for visa and immigration cases. Two or three days a week I'm also at a solicitors' office in town interpreting for clients. I work from a small desk in my studio flat, with a printer, a stamp and a folder of templates I made myself. I sign each page and the client pays a flat fee per page.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like how exact it is. A date on a birth certificate is either right or wrong, and I like being the person who makes sure it's right. What wears me out is chasing clients who want it tomorrow and then pay late, and the solicitors who book me for an hour and keep me for three without paying the extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was sensible of me not to rush into those tools. Certified work needs a signature and a person who takes responsibility, so it'd be business as usual. I wouldn't say much online, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd still be a bit worried, because the routine pages are exactly what software does well, and some clients would try it before coming to me. I'm still building up my client list and my rates are on the low side. One quiet month and I'm into my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and try to get on the approved list at a second solicitors' firm, which would give me steadier hours. I'd raise my page fee a little in January, from twenty-five to twenty-eight. And I'd keep three months of rent in the savings account and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A small knot in the stomach, but I've had that since I went freelance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one quiet month. Has that happened yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last August, when the immigration office was closed for two weeks, I earned about a third of a normal month. Nobody needed papers, and I had to dip into savings for the rent. My brother offered to help, but I didn't want to take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why didn't you want to take it from your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he has two small children and a car loan. I'd rather eat pasta for a month. I just made sure the rent went out on time.

I'd say **certified work** needs a signature and someone responsible, so business as usual.
think: Routine **certificate pages** are just what software does well, so some clients would try it.
My client list is **still small**, so one quiet month eats savings.
do: Get on the approved list at a **second solicitors' firm**.
Raise the **page fee** from twenty-five to twenty-eight in January.
Keep **three months of rent** untouched in savings.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with a small knot she's had since going freelance.

Won't take **family money** from her brother; pride and care for his children.

steps.text: Join the approved interpreter list at a second solicitors' firm
Raise the certified page fee from twenty-five to twenty-eight
Keep three months of rent untouched in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, carefully, that certified work still needs a human, and that clients should be wary of cheap online services. I'd tell the solicitors that if a translation is wrong in court, someone has to answer for it. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it starts to eat my work in two or three years. If the immigration office accepts AI translations with a quick human signature, the big online firms do it for five a page and I can't compete. The interpreting at the solicitors might hold, but there's only so much of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to get more interpreting hours, maybe at the courts, which means sitting the court interpreting test, around three hundred. I'd stop buying anything I don't need and push savings toward five months. I'd wait a bit before learning any of the AI tools, to see if they're actually accepted for certified work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's my plan for my life, and I can feel it getting thinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait before learning the tools. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the solicitors started asking me to check AI translations instead of doing my own. Then I'd have to, because that's the work. But I'd be slow, and I know I'd be slower than the younger people who already use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership and the Saturday coffee with my cousin, which I'd make a walk instead. I'd stop buying new clothes for work. I'd also stop sending a bit to my mum each month, which I'd hate.

**Wait** before learning AI tools until they're accepted.

fieldNote: She pins her hope on **rules about certification**, not on skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and make sure the rules for official papers are solid. I'd say it to the solicitors and to my family. I'm not someone who protests, but I'd sign a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think certified translation is gone by 2028 in that picture. If the AI is as good as any translator, the immigration office will just accept it, signature or not. All my work is thinking work, so the robots coming later doesn't matter to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to train for something steady, maybe a court clerk or an admin job in the immigration office, where my Arabic still helps. I'd save every bit I can and probably move back with my parents to stop paying rent. After it arrives, I'd lean on my family and whatever support the government offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Clerk and admin are thinking jobs too. Would that hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. You're right. I suppose I'd want something with people in a room, like a reception job at a clinic, where someone needs to be there in person. I honestly don't know what's safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents react to you moving back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would be pleased, though he'd never say it. My mum would start talking about marriage again. I'd survive it.

say: I'd ask for **solid rules** on official papers before anyone relies on AI.
I wouldn't protest, but I'd **sign a petition**.
think: **Certified translation** is gone by 2028 in this picture.
All my work is **thinking work**, so the robot delay doesn't help.
do: Train for a **steadier job** like clinic reception, where someone must be present.
Move back with her **parents** to stop paying rent.
Lean on **family and government** support once it arrives.
S2.quote: All my work is thinking work, so the robots coming later doesn't matter to me.
fieldNote: When challenged, she **admits she doesn't know** what's safe.
Moves from clerk to **in-person reception** after realising admin is thinking work too.
**Family** is her main safety net, with some humour about her mum.

steps.text: Train for clinic reception or similar in-person work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the government to set clear rules on certified papers. I'd say translators should get some say in that. I'd say it calmly, I'm not one for shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is hard for me, because I'm slow to change. I'd probably spend the first two years hoping it won't happen and then rush. I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd force myself to start something in year one, maybe a part-time healthcare admin course, around four hundred. I'd keep the certified work and the solicitors as long as they pay. And I'd ask my brother about working in his friend's pharmacy, since that's face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but it's slower. It's like a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hope it won't happen. What would stop you from hoping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the immigration office change its rules, I think. Once they accept an AI translation, it's real. Until then I'd keep telling myself it's years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger translator just starting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a younger translator not to buy a stamp and a printer like I did. Learn something else alongside, something with people. I wish someone had told me.

say: I'd ask the government for **clear rules** on certified papers within five years.
I'd say translators should **get a say**, calmly.
think: I'm **slow to change**, so I'd likely hope for two years, then rush.
Five years feels **hard** because of how I handle change.
do: Start a **healthcare admin course** in year one, about four hundred.
Keep **certified work** and the solicitors while they pay.
Ask her brother about the **pharmacy job** through his friend.
feel: **Alarmed**, though slower, like a bill she knows is coming.
S3.quote: I'd tell a younger translator not to buy a stamp and a printer like I did.
fieldNote: Strikingly **self-aware**: she predicts her own delay.

steps.text: Start a part-time healthcare admin course in year one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly. I'd want the immigration office and the courts to plan it with translators, not just switch over one day. I'd still not post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'd probably be okay. I'd have time to find a new path at my pace, which is slow. I'd be thirty-seven, which isn't old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating for maybe five years and slowly build a second skill, probably in healthcare, through evening classes. I'd save a bit more each month, maybe sixty. I'd wait a few years to see how things go before making a big jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but bearable. The kind of worry I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said at your pace. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One thing at a time. First the course, then maybe part-time work, then quitting translation. I don't like jumping without a net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the work you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The exactness. Checking a date three times. Somebody's whole visa can depend on one wrong number, and I'd miss being the person who catches it.

I'd say ten years is enough to **do it properly**.

At **thirty-seven** I'd still be young enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm slow and there'd be no time for me. What would help is clear notice from the immigration office about when they'll accept AI, and a funded course into healthcare. Even a year's notice would change a lot for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the clients. Most of them are scared people with their whole lives in a plastic folder. A machine can read the folder, but I'm not sure it'll notice when the client is shaking.

headlineQuote: A machine can read the folder, but I'm not sure it'll notice when the client is shaking.
portrait: A **27-year-old** Arabic–English certified translator working alone from her studio flat with a stamp and printer.
Never uses **AI tools** and admits she's slow to change.
Already lives with **lumpy income**, so AI Plateau leaves her uneasy.
Pins hope on **certification rules**, then plans a slow move into healthcare.
Leans on **family** as her safety net, without wanting to burden her brother.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as there'd be no time for someone slow to change.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice** from the immigration office about accepting AI.
